'''Russell David Gray''' is a New Zealand evolutionary [[Biologist]] and [[Psychologist]] working on applying quantitative methods to the study of cultural evolution and human prehistory. He is a Director at the [[Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology]] in [[Leipzig]], where he heads the Department of Linguistic and Cultural Evolution, and holds an adjunct position in the School of Psychology at the [[University of Auckland]].<ref name = MPIEVAbio>{{cite web |last1=Gray |first1=Russell |url=https://www.eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/staff/russell-gray/ |website=Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology |access-date=3 Dec 2021|title=Russell Gray}}</ref> He is known for the application of [[computational phylogenetics|computational phylogenetic]] methods to the study of language families including [[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]] and [[Austronesian languages|Austronesian]], and for research on tool manufacture in [[New Caledonian crow]]s.

== Career ==
Gray completed his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] at the [[University of Auckland]] in 1990.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Gray |first=Russell |year=1990 |type=Doctoral thesis |title=Design, constraint and construction: essays and experiments on evolution and foraging |publisher=ResearchSpace@Auckland, University of Auckland |hdl=2292/1852}}</ref> He spent four years lecturing at the [[University of Otago]], New Zealand, before returning to the School of Psychology at the [[University of Auckland]]. He is a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of New Zealand]] and has been awarded with several fellowships, as well as the inaugural [[Mason Durie (psychiatrist)#Achievements|Mason Durie Medal]] (in 2012) for his pioneering contributions to social science.<ref name="royalsociety.org.nz">{{cite web |title=Recipients of the Mason Durie Medal |url=https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/what-we-do/medals-and-awards/mason-durie-medal/recipients-3/ |website=Royal Society Te Apārangi |access-date=3 Dec 2021}}</ref> In 2014, he became one of the two founding directors of the [[Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History]] in Jena, Germany, where he established and headed the Department of Linguistic and Cultural Evolution. In 2020 the department relocated to the [[Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology]] in Leipzig, where Gray was appointed a Director. He also holds adjunct positions in the School of Psychology at the University of Auckland and the Department of Philosophy at the [[Australian National University]].<ref name="MPIEVAbio" />

Gray's doctoral thesis was titled ''Design, constraint and construction: essays and experiments on evolution and foraging''.<ref>{{Cite Q|Q111963797}}</ref>

Notable students of Gray include [[Simon Greenhill]].<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Greenhill |first=Simon |year=2008 |type=Doctoral thesis |title=The archives of history : a phylogenetic approach to the study of language |publisher=ResearchSpace@Auckland, University of Auckland |hdl=2292/51143}}</ref>

== Evolutionary linguistics and cultural evolution ==
Gray was among the researchers who applied [[Computational phylogenetics|phylogenetic methods]] developed in evolutionary biology to problems in [[historical linguistics]]. In 2000, with Fiona Jordan, he used language trees to test competing models of the [[Austronesian peoples|Austronesian]] expansion into the Pacific.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gray |first1=Russell D. |last2=Jordan |first2=Fiona M. |year=2000 |title=Language trees support the express-train sequence of Austronesian expansion |journal=Nature |volume=405 |pages=1052–1055 |doi=10.1038/35016575|hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0013-3698-A |hdl-access=free }}</ref> In 2003, with his doctoral student [[Quentin Atkinson]], he applied Bayesian phylogenetic dating to the disputed question of [[Proto-Indo-European homeland|Indo-European origins]], reporting divergence dates consistent with an Anatolian farming expansion.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gray |first1=Russell D. |last2=Atkinson |first2=Quentin D. |year=2003 |title=Language-tree divergence times support the Anatolian theory of Indo-European origin |journal=Nature |volume=426 |pages=435–439 |doi=10.1038/nature02029}}</ref> The study was widely discussed and contested, both on the question of Indo-European origins and on the use of phylogenetic methods in linguistics.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Balter |first=Michael |year=2003 |title=Early date for the birth of Indo-European languages |journal=Science |volume=302 |issue=5650 |pages=1490–1491 |doi=10.1126/science.302.5650.1490a |pmid=14645820}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Chang|first1=Will|last2=Cathcart|first2=Chundra|last3=Hall|first3=David|last4=Garrett|first4=Andrew|title=Ancestry-constrained Phylogenetic Analysis Supports the Indo-European Steppe Hypothesis|journal=Language|date=2015|volume=91|number=1|pages=194–244|doi=10.1353/lan.2015.0005|s2cid=143978664|url=http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/9cr00162}}</ref>

With [[Alexei Drummond]] and Simon Greenhill, Gray used a database of Austronesian basic vocabulary to reconstruct the settlement of the Pacific, describing a sequence of expansion pulses and pauses.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gray |first1=Russell D. |last2=Drummond |first2=Alexei J. |last3=Greenhill |first3=Simon J. |year=2009 |title=Language phylogenies reveal expansion pulses and pauses in Pacific settlement |journal=Science |volume=323 |pages=479–483 |doi=10.1126/science.1166858}}</ref> A 2011 study of which he was a co-author compared word-order features across four language families and reported lineage-specific rather than universal patterns of change.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dunn |first1=Michael |display-authors=etal |year=2011 |title=Evolved structure of language shows lineage-specific trends in word-order universals |journal=Nature |volume=473 |pages=79–82 |doi=10.1038/nature09923|hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0013-3B19-B |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Gray is project leader of [[Grambank]], a database of grammatical features compiled for comparative analysis, and a member of the team behind Lexibank, a collection of standardised lexical datasets.<ref>https://www.eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/grambank/</ref> The initial global analysis of Grambank reported strong genealogical structuring of grammatical diversity and assessed the loss of structural diversity associated with language endangerment.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Skirgård |first1=Hedvig |display-authors=etal |year=2023 |title=Grambank reveals the importance of genealogical constraints on linguistic diversity and highlights the impact of language loss |journal=Science Advances |volume=9 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adg6175|hdl=10150/673832 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

A 2023 study co-authored by Gray combined an expanded Indo-European lexical dataset with ancient DNA evidence to argue for an origin south of the Caucasus, with subsequent spread of some branches through the Pontic–Caspian steppe.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Heggarty |first1=Paul |display-authors=etal |year=2023 |title=Language trees with sampled ancestors support a hybrid model for the origin of Indo-European languages |journal=Science |volume=381 |doi=10.1126/science.abg0818}}</ref>

== Animal cognition ==
Gray has conducted research on tool manufacture and use in [[New Caledonian crow]]s. Working with Gavin Hunt at the University of Auckland, he studied the form, geographical distribution and development of the birds' tool-making. A 2001 study with Hunt and [[Michael Corballis]] reported population-level laterality in tool manufacture.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hunt |first1=Gavin R. |last2=Corballis |first2=Michael C. |last3=Gray |first3=Russell D. |title=Laterality in tool manufacture by crows |journal=Nature |volume=414 |year=2001 |page=707 |doi=10.1038/414707a}}</ref> Later work considered whether variation in tool design reflects cultural transmission and cumulative modification.

Experimental work by the Auckland group examined the cognitive mechanisms involved, including metatool use, causal reasoning and planning. A 2007 experiment reported that the crows could spontaneously use one tool to obtain another.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Taylor |first1=Alex H. |last2=Hunt |first2=Gavin R. |last3=Holzhaider |first3=Jennifer C. |last4=Gray |first4=Russell D. |title=Spontaneous metatool use by New Caledonian crows |journal=Current Biology |volume=17 |year=2007 |pages=1504–1507 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2007.07.057}}</ref> Subsequent experiments tested whether their performance reflected causal understanding or simpler associative learning.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gruber |first1=Romana |last2=Schiestl |first2=Martina |last3=Boeckle |first3=Markus |last4=Frohnwieser |first4=Anna |last5=Miller |first5=Rachael |last6=Gray |first6=Russell D. |last7=Clayton |first7=Nicola S. |last8=Taylor |first8=Alex H. |title=New Caledonian crows use mental representations to solve metatool problems |journal=Current Biology |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=686–692.e3 |date=18 February 2019 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2019.01.008 |pmid=30744978|pmc=6384166 }}</ref>

== Honours ==

Gray was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of New Zealand]] in 2008.<ref>https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/who-we-are/our-people/our-fellows/view-our-fellows</ref> In 2002 he was awarded a [[James Cook Research Fellowship]],<ref>https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/what-we-do/funds-and-opportunities/james-cook-research-fellowship/james-cook-research-fellowships-recipients/search-james-cook-fellowship-awards?start=70</ref> and in 2012 he received the inaugural Mason Durie Medal,<ref>https://pacific.scoop.co.nz/2012/11/new-medal-for-social-science-at-2012-nz-research-honours/</ref> awarded for advances at the frontiers of social science; in its citation the Society credited him with pioneering the systematic application of evolutionary thinking and computational methods to questions of language, cognition and culture.<ref name="royalsociety.org.nz"/>
